section.title: Michael Novati: Early Facebook, the Coding Machine, and Reaching Senior Staff
section.deck: Michael Novati, an early Facebook engineer who rose to senior staff, argues that output was constant over a career and that taste, trust, and feedback loops are what moved him up.

blocks.text: Michael Novati joined Facebook as an intern in 2009, when the company had roughly 200 engineers, and later reached senior staff (IC7). In this interview Novati argues that raw coding output was already high in the first week and barely changed over the career. What moved Novati up the ladder was accumulated taste and judgment, built through repeated feedback, plus the credibility to make wide-reaching changes safely. The host, who is not named in the captions, also asks about early Facebook culture, stories about Mark Zuckerberg, whether LLMs threaten the coding-machine archetype, and why Novati left Meta. Everything below is Novati's account and opinion unless marked as an editorial note.
blocks.heading: Novati's view: output gets an engineer started, but judgment, trust, and feedback loops carry the career

blocks.question: What was the story behind joining Facebook as an intern, and why that company when it was small?
answer: Novati started as an intern in May 2009, between undergrad and grad school. A PhD in human-computer interaction at the University of Washington was already planned, with housing and a research assistantship lined up. Novati wanted work experience at a top company doing interesting product work, and applied online only to Facebook and Google. Getting interviews was not hard then, Novati says, and seems harder now.

The Facebook fit was close to accidental. Novati happened to interview with an engineer building internal collaboration tools: diff review, tasks, and discussion. That was the kind of "social network for work" Novati most wanted to build. After doing well on the LeetCode-style questions, Novati joined that engineer's team, with that engineer as manager. Novati calls it the stars aligning.

followups.question: How big was the company then in terms of engineers?
answer: About 220, Novati says, with a caveat. Production engineers were not classified as software engineers at the time, so the exact count depends on how the line is drawn. Roughly 200 is the safe figure.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What drew Novati so strongly to Meta's culture?
answer: Novati names a technical pull and a social one. On day one, following the setup instructions, the dev environment ran Apache and PHP locally against a MySQL database, much like a side project, only with a larger federated database behind it. Novati says it felt like home and in tune with how the company built things.

Socially, Facebook was a product everyone had heard of and had opinions on. Novati could get plenty of feedback about what people liked and disliked, and found it motivating to build something people cared about. Novati adds that the company went through ups and downs, even during the tenure.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Many engineers who joined then were put off by PHP. Did Novati feel the same?
answer: Novati gives a split answer: yes and no. Meta now mainly uses Hack, a derivative of PHP, and the path there took stages. The first was a compiler that turned PHP into faster code. There was also a debate about rewriting the whole codebase in Java or Python, and the company chose to optimize and customize the language instead. Novati recalls type-related changes, described as "loose typing", among the early additions.

Off-the-shelf PHP carried a stigma at the time. Novati's reading of Facebook's approach was to make the language better than any other could be for this company, by customizing it at the language level so it was easier for engineers and faster. The host adds a view of their own, that PHP gets more criticism than it deserves and that Hack is a much better experience.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What does Novati think of "move fast and break things," now that the culture has changed?
answer: Novati describes having been "the move fast and break things person" at the time and still likes the framing. In Novati's reading, the "break things" half was partly an outside perception, and Facebook did not want to tell the public that people were recklessly breaking everything. The original spirit was breaking norms: first-principles thinking, trying things from scratch, not following trends for their own sake. It was not meant as causing havoc.

Novati still thinks it would be a fine motto today. At a larger, more mature company, though, even the smallest bug can cost millions or tens of millions of dollars, so Novati can see why the company dropped it.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did the culture change over the years, given that Novati started when there were about 200 engineers?
answer: Novati describes an extremely engineer-driven culture. Designers and product managers had to win engineers over, because work an engineer would not build did not get built. Nearly all internal tools were written in-house and used by employees, which set an engineering-first tone that Novati loved.

Novati sees the 2012 IPO as a turning point. The stock fell afterward because people asked how Facebook would make money, a question that had barely come up in the first three years. As the company grew, Novati developed a more mature view: ad optimization, cost savings, and efficient infrastructure became more important. Early on, senior engineers argued out designs head-to-head, largely independent of management. By the end, VPs of two teams more often negotiated and the result percolated down.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What was the mood at the IPO? Ecstatic, or scared by the stock drop?
answer: Not scared, Novati says. It was celebratory but grounded. Zuckerberg was good, early on, at keeping things humble and not chasing press or perception. Novati describes the IPO as a rational way to raise funding rather than a party, yet still something that pulled employees together. Nasdaq brought the bell button to campus and a stage was set up. Novati says there was a story about how it was wired up and suggests asking internally.

Zuckerberg's parents stood right beside Novati in the crowd, with tears in their eyes, and Novati later told Zuckerberg about it. Novati found the moment impactful. Financially, nothing changed at first, because the stock vested about six months after the IPO.

followups.question: What was it like when the stock vested after it had fallen?
answer: Novati remembers the day clearly. About 20 colleagues were at a movie theater when phones went off all at once with notices that vested stock had been deposited. The IPO changed little in behavior over the short term. Over a longer horizon, Novati says, people could afford houses and children in the expensive Bay Area.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did Novati hold the stock, or diversify as soon as it vested?
answer: Novati held the IPO-era shares and still has all of them. At some later point, Novati says, vested shares were sold as they vested in order to diversify; the timing is not remembered. Novati was grateful for classes, taught by veterans of the Google and Yahoo IPOs, on managing finances and stock-based compensation. Having grown up in Canada, Novati had not deeply understood stock pay and found the lessons on risk "infinitely helpful".

followups.question: Was Novati sweating when Meta stock fell to around 90?
answer: A little, Novati says. Holdings were diversified enough that retirement was not at stake. The host notes the price had been around 150 to 180 when the host joined in 2018.

Novati draws a lesson for people comparing offers, from watching stock swings. Novati knows people who joined during the dip and saw their stock rise nearly sixfold in about three years (Novati's own estimate). Candidates often compare offers in today's dollars and agonize over single-digit percentage gaps. Novati calls it reasonable to care, but stresses that the numbers are estimates and that stock prices, acquisitions, and scandals are outside anyone's control. Novati advises prioritizing the company where the candidate will fit and perform well, because performance is more within one's control and is rewarded over time. The host adds that early in a career, a single promotion can mean about 40 percent more pay.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What was the internal newsletter that made Novati well known, and why start it?
answer: It was called "the weekly Novati", a weekly post on the Notes product, Facebook's blogging feature. Notes had no owner when Novati joined in 2009, so Novati improved it at hackathons, adding rich text to what had been plain text. The change was an 11,000-line diff, so large that Novati had to organize an in-person meeting to review it. Novati also used the product constantly, as part of Facebook's dogfooding habit.

A few slightly controversial posts about product building drew traction, so Novati posted more regularly, often off the cuff. Facebook was adamant about staying on the Menlo Park campus, while startups such as Stripe and Uber in San Francisco were drawing employees away. Novati wrote repeatedly about it, including a post proposing a South San Francisco office, and that office later opened.

followups.question: Would Novati recommend an internal newsletter like that today?
answer: Overall, Novati says, no. There was no strategic reason to write it. It came from Facebook's value of being open and transparent: Novati wanted to strip away pleasantries and look at products honestly, for example admitting when a product grew through luck and not substance. Novati contrasts this with startups and boot camps that treat a little traction as proof they built something great. The posts had nothing to do with performance reviews or influence.

The cost was friction. Novati once openly called out that engineers with titles such as network engineer or data engineer could not move between teams as easily as software engineers. Novati did not realize it was a sore point behind the scenes, and executives said the post did not help and that they now had damage control to do. Novati's lesson is that an off-the-cuff style has consequences, though Novati still tries to be direct and open on Reddit and LinkedIn.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Did HR ever ask Novati to take posts down?
answer: Nothing took the form of a takedown order, Novati says, but HR did give feedback. One post covered which companies were poaching Facebook engineers, and Uber was then offering very large stock grants. HR pointed out it might unintentionally encourage people to explore other jobs. Novati had not thought of that and says such off-the-cuff posts may not have been worth the friction.
Concerned, Novati messaged Zuckerberg directly. Zuckerberg was fine with it and encouraged Novati to keep posting.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Could Novati really message Zuckerberg directly and get a reply?
answer: Yes. Facebook was small when Novati joined, and Novati dealt regularly with the executives. When leaving, Novati messaged each executive one-on-one, including Chris Cox, and says they replied with thanks. Novati felt a relationship with all of them, formed from interacting genuinely while the company was small, and got to know Zuckerberg best, partly outside work. Novati has not spoken with many of them in the past couple of years as Facebook has grown.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Did Zuckerberg still write code when Novati joined, and did Novati ever see a diff from him?
answer: Novati worked with Zuckerberg on a 2009 hackathon project built on Zuckerberg's idea that anyone should be able to react to any post with any emoji. Novati was skeptical but thought it feasible. Novati and another engineer got a version working, but the code was so bad it never shipped. Zuckerberg did not give up, and when reactions launched later under a product manager, Novati thought it was done properly and so much better than Zuckerberg's code.

Novati also tells a story from a 2010 lockdown, when Facebook worried a rival product (the captions say only "plus") might dent its user base and pushed to ship features fast. At a company-wide Q&A, Novati bet Zuckerberg would not commit code by the end of lockdown, and offered to stop riding a Ripstik around the office if he did. Zuckerberg committed it, and Novati was banned from riding. Roughly 2012, Novati adds, the head of HR emailed the five most prominent riders for feedback on a draft email banning Ripstiks, a classic way to win over opponents.

followups.question: When Novati first arrived, could you see the founders' names in the codebase history?
answer: Occasionally, yes. In company lore, the earliest engineers were not known for the best-quality code, but they wrote fast and did the job. Later a wave of more experienced engineers arrived, including some poached from Microsoft, and began laying down structure and framework. Others wrote the core abstractions that became the foundation for the product infrastructure team, which Novati says existed for a very long time. Their names were all over the codebase, including Evan Priestley's, and they were Novati's role models when Novati wanted to become the coding machine who writes a lot of code.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Which engineers impressed Novati most, and why?
answer: The product infrastructure team, which built PHP abstractions that evolved into today's React framework. Novati watched the framework go up brick by brick and saw those engineers as a different type, a specialty that was not Novati's. The person most like Novati was Evan Priestley, who Novati says was the top committer before Novati. Priestley wrote the internal code-review suite essentially alone, and it was later forked and open sourced (the captions render its name unclearly).

followups.question: Would Novati choose Priestley or four regular senior engineers for a new product team?
answer: Priestley. Novati then qualifies it as context-dependent. Being called a coding machine is not magic: it comes from hard work, from holding a lot of code in memory, and from attention to the littlest details. Novati says that on Oculus firmware, productivity would be slow at first. In a comfortable codebase where everyone has ramped up, Novati would pick the coding machine. For something truly new, a more diverse group may bring more flexibility and creativity. A coding machine, Novati says, makes things happen that people thought impossible.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Can Novati give an example a team of seven senior engineers would not have finished?
answer: Novati's canonical example is a framework called Preparables. A component had a data-fetching function and a rendering function, so all data could be fetched in parallel before rendering. It was later replaced by async/await and more modern approaches. Thousands of classes used it, and Novati manually and relentlessly refactored every one away, roughly three to six thousand by Novati's estimate, until the parent class was gone. It took several months and was a solo effort.

A second project removed every direct PHP endpoint hit on the server in favor of the routing framework. Neither was the company's top priority, Novati says, and without personal drive they would have consumed resources better spent on new products. One person doing them made all engineers' lives easier by removing legacy frameworks.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Will LLMs kill the coding machine archetype, given that a large refactor like that sounds doable by an LLM?
answer: Novati did the Facebook work in Vim, with an in-house indexed code search tool and a class-name tab-completion plugin, and was very productive. Modern editors would have made Novati more so. Novati sees LLM tools as the next step, like going from Vim to VS Code: they make refactors and changes faster. Agentic flows are emerging with some success cases but are not mainstream.

In Novati's view, most engineers still use AI tools much less than those at the leading edge. If everyone used them the way leaders do, the industry would already have changed massively, coding machines included. How agentic flows will affect coding machines and everyone else, Novati says, is undecided.

followups.question: What is the biggest difference between the old Vim workflow and working with LLMs?
answer: Novati works in a roughly 500,000-line codebase and still knows most of its structure, so multi-file agentic flows are used only occasionally. The main use is speeding up code Novati already knows how to write. For something like a 100-line page component, Novati makes a real-time call about whether typing it or prompting it is faster, and builds up prompting intuition prompt by prompt.

Novati says the product workflow is similar to six months earlier but code output is about five times higher (Novati's own estimate). There is no fixed endgame, Novati adds, since each new model or command-line tool brings new intuitions.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: How would Novati feel if coding became a hobby and programming was no longer driven by humans?
answer: Novati thinks it is a cool future. Clocked honestly, much engineering time is copy-paste, searching, and staring at the screen. Without that, engineers could focus on the fun parts: creative product work, and for Novati the joy of cleaning up code and merging unrelated things into one concept. Novati offers Sergey Brin dropping into whatever he wants to work on as a model.

Novati also finds it scary for the profession, because it raises the question of what being a software engineer means: writing code, designing data models, systems work, or gluing things together. For the near term, Novati is more confident that experienced engineers with strong taste become more productive and that building that experience gets harder for newcomers.

Beyond that, if AI writes and maintains its own code, Novati expects it will not look like today's code. It might manage services behind contractual APIs, in code no one reads. Novati expects the change to come step by step, not as an overnight dystopia, and says people should try to make that world as good as possible and not push back.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What impressed Novati about the React-framework engineers, whose archetype differed from Novati's?
answer: Novati files them under the specialist archetype: people very good at one stack. Another example is an engineer who was one of perhaps ten people in the world who deeply understood email protocols, including the practical side of spam and routing. Novati likes a sports-team analogy: on a baseball team every player can play most positions reasonably, yet you want distinct roles and mutual respect for each player's place. Novati respects those engineers and sees the team as exceptional when it has different kinds of players.

followups.question: Was it that they solved problems others could not?
answer: Yes, Novati says, and their abstractions were especially impactful because every engineer used them daily. Novati's own cleanup work also eased everyone's life, so there was some similarity. Their frameworks cut the mental overhead of tasks such as fetching data. Novati notes that an elegant, fast, easy-to-use API is very hard to design, and that making things simpler can be more work than writing a lot of code.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Novati has said about 30 percent of time went to the team and 70 percent to self-directed projects. How does that work?
answer: Novati frames it as being a senior engineer on a team of about ten while spending more than half the time on codebase-wide initiatives: cleanups, refactors, a new framework, one-off help, and emergencies. The 30 percent was a share of mental focus, not a slice of the eight-hour day. Novati was on the team all day, reviewing code, bouncing ideas off junior engineers, mentoring them toward promotion, and writing features the team had queued. Novati also joined product meetings and assessed feasibility of what product managers proposed. The volume of code from team work was that of a senior engineer.

followups.question: How did Novati manage the relationship with the manager, given that most bandwidth went elsewhere?
answer: Novati often, though not always, reported to more junior managers and acted almost as a peer who helped them manage the team. The skip-level manager usually did the performance reviews, and Novati effectively reported to that skip unofficially. Novati met a VP monthly for the whole org and the skip every two weeks. On the org chart Novati reported to a frontline manager, but in practice Novati was a dotted-line resource for senior people, "a weapon of the org" that went wherever needed.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: How did Novati transition into IC7, solving the hardest problems for the whole org?
answer: Novati says output was already at coding-machine level from day one. What improved was taste and judgment. As an example, there were two forks of the task tool on the same data source, one fast and streamlined, one bloated with features and slow. In a week or less, Novati merged them into one with the speed of the first and the features of the second. Novati told no one, posted to the whole company that the tools were merged, and says this could not be done now.

Everyone congratulated Novati, but the lesson was that surprising hundreds of users with changed URLs was not the best way. Novati had not understood the consequences for teams. Over many large changes, some too fast and some buggy, Novati kept the same speed while improving judgment: how much to change at once, what other people will feel, and which spots are sensitive. That accumulation of judgment and taste is what crosses the line into IC7, Novati says. Advice on building it depends on context: talk to a manager, then a skip-level manager, then a very senior engineer in a similar org.

followups.question: So high productivity and initiative let Novati take on extra work and become known for it?
answer: Yes, Novati says, but judgment and taste matter more than the code. They extend to the push process. Facebook had no continuous integration then. If something broke in production, the pushing team had to ship a fix, and an engineer who broke too much lost its trust, which would hurt a coding machine. Novati built that relationship, and more than once said a change needed to land and that if it broke the site Novati would resign. Novati had burned credibility before, so had to be very sure of the fix. An engineer who simply writes a lot of code, without years of built-up trust, could not get away with it.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

followups.question: Would Novati have resigned if it had broken again?
answer: Novati thinks so. The statement puts so much pressure on Novati, perhaps a personality trait, that Novati triple-checks every line and thinks through every odd case.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What do taste and judgment mean for a software engineer?
answer: Novati likens taste to the patina on a cast-iron pan, built up in layers of history. Some people have stronger instincts early, perhaps from upbringing or from experience outside code such as dancing or sports. In general it takes experience. Novati's second image is a speed skater: you cannot read a book, put on skates, and be fastest. It takes years of feeling the ice at different temperatures and the difference between a skate used once and twice.

Novati sees too many people early in their careers trying to jump ahead, like entering the Olympics before building that feel. That is okay, Novati says, and nothing is wrong with them. The advice is to put in practice and reps, get feedback, iterate, and have the grit to keep going; without feedback, practice does not improve skill.

followups.question: Is taste about how to design software, or about which problems are worth solving?
answer: Both, for different people, Novati says. A product manager's taste is mostly about what to build, built by shipping many things and watching some fail. Novati says the exceptional ones have shipped mostly things that failed or were mediocre, and learned at each step (a loose, unmeasured claim). For an engineer, Novati says, taste applies to the code itself and to strategies for moving fast.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Novati was touching everyone's code. Did other teams give feedback, and how was it handled?
answer: Yes. In one case Novati refactored an old framework in the live version of a team's tool while that team was building a newer tool and carefully maintaining backward compatibility. They had many diffs in flight, and the refactor caused merge conflicts. They wanted it reverted. Novati had not paid attention to that, and the lesson is to be careful where teams are mid-migration on complex, longer-term work.

followups.question: Did anyone object that Novati added something without owning its maintenance?
answer: That never came up, Novati says. The philosophy then, which Novati reports Kent Beck also described recently, was that every line you write you are responsible for. If you are willing to be woken at 3 a.m. to fix your code, you can skip tests. If you want to work nine to five, write more tests so the code is stable while you are away.

Novati did not refactor and forget. Sometimes two years later an automatic bug would be assigned because Novati had touched the code last, and Novati fixed it as now Novati's. Novati had no territorial conflicts and did not step on people's product judgment. Novati compares it to surgery, learned the hard way through early over-aggressiveness: finding the line between disrupting people's day-to-day work and still getting the cleanup done.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: As engineers get more senior they are pulled into more meetings. How did Novati protect focus time?
answer: Novati minimized meetings. When calendar invites arrived without context, Novati asked what they were for and pushed back on many. Novati skipped standups unless relevant, for example during a crunch to ship within a month, and did not attend ones that were social chitchat. Novati was strict about time and chose teams deliberately, valuing managers who understood that their job is to help reports perform exceptionally. Novati's managers protected Novati from unnecessary meetings so impact could be highest.
Novati admits being too arrogant at times. Novati recalls walking out of a meeting or two after deciding it was no longer useful, and now regrets it, feeling bad for whoever ran the meeting.

followups.question: Did HR ever ask Novati to be nicer?
answer: No, Novati says, because it was not a table-flipping situation. Novati had good relationships with the product managers, who liked that Novati built and fixed things fast, including bugs that were not Novati's. Meta's product managers want things moving fast and watch every pixel. They would often give Novati permission to leave when a meeting no longer needed Novati. Novati describes the attitude as cutthroat about not spending time in meetings when Novati could be coding.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: How did Novati develop the skill of picking problems that mattered, so the code was more impactful?
answer: Novati says first that Novati is not great at it and is still poor at prioritizing. Novati tended to pick things where Novati could already see the answer, so the only question was how fast the code could be typed. That is also why LLMs help Novati so much: the idea is in Novati's head and the tool gets it out faster.

Novati calls this one of the things that probably held back the career. When a manager asked for task A, and Novati could not see the answer, Novati did B through H instead. That earns a passing grade and is appreciated, but if A really mattered, the company's overall impact would likely have been higher had Novati done it. Novati frames it as a weakness, limited by what Novati can figure out how to do.

followups.question: So the priority list was whatever Novati could crank out instantly, not full business value?
answer: Novati agrees and adds that if you crank out enough, it adds up and can have huge impact, but it is a different way of thinking about work.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What did the IC7-plus engineers have in common?
answer: Novati says there was a common bar regardless of archetype, whether coding machine, specialist, or fixer. Everyone showed extremely strong diligence and conscientiousness, and was sharp. Novati cites a straight-A school record and a sense of being fairly smart, yet acknowledges that many in the group are probably smarter. In a room, a newly proposed protocol would not get an hour-long presentation; people would ask sharp follow-up questions at once. Attention to detail was very high.

For Novati these are personality traits, such as using obsessive tendencies productively on every detail of the product. Others reached them through 25 years of experience. In conversations with junior colleagues, Novati says, context is often missing, follow-ups are less sharp and take longer, and projects are usually smaller in scope.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What are the top tips for landing code fast, for someone who wants to absorb the coding-machine skill?
answer: Novati's step one is to do something, anything. Many people who ask for advice think too much and do too little. Step two, which Novati calls critical, is to get feedback from respected people with experience, taste, and judgment, act on it, and repeat. Novati once thought a manager hated Novati because the manager spent all day reviewing a flood of fast, problem-filled code and kept asking for style conventions to be followed. Novati says that annoyance is the loop working: get the gears turning, take the feedback, iterate. It compounds quickly.

Novati names three mistakes. The first is not turning the gears at all. The second is getting feedback from the wrong people, such as a boot-camp graduate taking feedback from a peer only slightly ahead, which lacks the experience and taste one wants to learn. The third, which Novati made often, is treating feedback as judgment or approval and not as information. The host summarizes it as shortening the cycle time, getting good feedback, and internalizing it.

followups.question: For someone already productive, what advice takes things to the next level?
answer: Be more ambitious. Take on something that pushes beyond the normal scope. Novati says this is specific to Meta, where impact is judged by breadth and scope, so a coding machine in a department needs to push beyond it. The advice Novati gives, despite saying Novati is poor at accepting leaders' prioritization, is to reach out to senior people in other areas. Novati had many one-on-ones with the senior leadership, such as a 15-minute chat with Chris Cox, and says a credible but stuck coding machine can use such talks to find wider-scoped projects.
followups.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: Why did Novati leave Meta, and what was the career thinking?
answer: Novati says Meta got big fast. Around three-quarters of the way through the tenure, the feeling faded that the company had Novati's back completely and Novati had the company's, a feeling Novati admits was a bit culty. It started to feel like a business relationship, and that was the first sign Novati was open to leaving.

Vesting logistics sharpened it. Some years had longer grants and overlapping vesting cycles, and Novati expected take-home pay to drop about 80 percent over a period (Novati's own figure; details withheld). After the previous performance cycle, Novati told the manager that Novati would leave in three months, did a farewell tour on a Messenger-for-kids project, and slowly ramped down, taking things home from the desk. Novati describes being either all-in or not, says that all-in feeling broke as Meta grew, and wanted to put the dedication elsewhere.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: At the highest levels of performance, how much is talent and how much is hard work and growth?
answer: Talent exists, Novati says, shaped by biology, upbringing, and opportunity, and some of it is undiscovered. Someone who feels untalented may simply not have found it yet, or may be talented at something that is not their day job. Novati says this is the mission behind the current work of helping people find the most impactful work they can do, since not everyone had the chance to explore. Novati believes everyone is better than most at something, and finding it is a big piece of high performance.

Hard work, in contrast, is within your control. A friend of Novati's makes the point that talent and luck are outside your control and effort is not. If you are good at your job and like it, Novati says, you can outwork similar people and will probably be recognized for it.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What percent of Novati's career growth is luck?
answer: Novati says 50/50. Coming from Canada, Novati's first day at Facebook was a surprise: Novati took a laptop and left onboarding, and was called back because Novati had not collected a phone. Facebook handed over a phone and accessories as if rolling out a red carpet, and Novati wondered what it all was. Staying in Canada would probably have gone well, Novati says, but without the same acceleration.

The luck was landing at Facebook when Novati did: a perfect fit for Novati's personality then, aligned values, and code that matched what Novati could handle. Novati has seen people without the same drive who got the luck and are doing well, and says either factor can work out. Novati says both applied here.
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati

blocks.question: What advice would Novati give to a just-graduated self?
answer: Novati sees many people, including those preparing for interviews, seeking approval: a green check mark, a perfect grade. Novati was that person, wanting an A+ without really knowing what was being learned. Because of that, Novati treated feedback as a grade to judge by and not as input for improving, and pressured toward 100 percent next time instead of toward improvement.
